section.title: Bricks Without Straw
section.sectionRationale: One continuous scene of escalating conflict, from the first audience with Pharaoh through his punitive new policy to the foremen's despair and Moses' own anguished prayer, ending just before God's renewed promise in chapter 6.
section.thesis: Pharaoh's flat refusal, 'I do not know the LORD,' brings not relief but harsher bondage, and even Moses is driven to complain that God has made things worse, showing that deliverance often grows darkest just before God moves.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: the first demand and Pharaoh's contemptuous refusal; the harsher policy of bricks without straw; the foremen's complaint and Moses' anguished prayer.

verses.text: After that, Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.’”
But Pharaoh replied, “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go.”

“The God of the Hebrews has met with us,” they answered. “Please let us go on a three-day journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to the LORD our God, or He may strike us with plagues or with the sword.”
But the king of Egypt said to them, “Moses and Aaron, why do you draw the people away from their work? Get back to your labor!”
Pharaoh also said, “Look, the people of the land are now numerous, and you would be stopping them from their labor.”
That same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their foremen:
“You shall no longer supply the people with {{teben|straw}} for making bricks. They must go and gather their own straw.
But require of them the same quota of bricks as before; do not reduce it. For they are lazy; that is why they are crying out, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’
Make the {{avodah|work}} harder on the men so they will be occupied and pay no attention to these lies.”
So the taskmasters and foremen of the people went out and said to them, “This is what Pharaoh says: ‘I am no longer giving you straw.
Go and get your own straw wherever you can find it; but your workload will in no way be reduced.’”
So the people scattered all over the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.
The taskmasters kept pressing them, saying, “Fulfill your quota each day, just as you did when straw was provided.”
Then the Israelite foremen, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over the people, were beaten and asked, “Why have you not fulfilled your quota of bricks yesterday or today, as you did before?”
So the Israelite foremen went and appealed to Pharaoh: “Why are you treating your servants this way?
No straw has been given to your servants, yet we are told, ‘Make bricks!’ Look, your servants are being beaten, but the fault is with your own people.”
“You are slackers!” Pharaoh replied. “Slackers! That is why you keep saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.’
Now get to work. You will be given no straw, yet you must deliver the full quota of bricks.”
The Israelite foremen realized they were in trouble when they were told, “You must not reduce your daily quota of bricks.”
When they left Pharaoh, they confronted Moses and Aaron, who stood waiting to meet them.
“May the LORD look upon you and judge you,” the foremen said, “for you have made us a stench before Pharaoh and his officials; you have placed in their hand a sword to kill us!”
So Moses returned to the LORD and asked, “Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people? Is this why You sent me?
Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in Your name, he has brought trouble on this people, and You have not delivered Your people in any way.”

teben.gloss: Straw or chopped stubble, mixed into clay to bind mud bricks. Withholding it while demanding the same quota was a calculated cruelty, forcing the Israelites to waste labor gathering material that had previously been supplied.

avodah.gloss: Work, labor, or service. The same word can describe both slavery to Pharaoh and worship service to the LORD; the whole conflict of Exodus turns on whose avodah Israel will render, Pharaoh's crushing labor or God's freeing worship.

basic.context: Moses and Aaron finally confront Pharaoh with God's demand to let Israel go, and Pharaoh flatly refuses, mocking the LORD's name. Instead of relief, things get worse: Pharaoh punishes Israel by forcing them to gather their own straw for bricks while keeping the same daily quota. The Israelite foremen are beaten, and they blame Moses, who in turn cries out to God in anguish.
basic.hermeneutics: This is honest historical narrative that does not smooth over how hard obedience can be. It shows that following God's call does not guarantee immediate relief, and it is not shy about recording Moses' raw complaint to God when things seemed to go from bad to worse.
basic.originalLanguages: Pharaoh withholds teben, straw, while keeping the brick quota, a deliberate cruelty. The whole conflict turns on avodah, a word meaning both slave labor and worship service, since Israel's crisis is precisely a battle over whose avodah, whose service, they will render.
basic.typology: Israel's cry for relief that instead brings harsher bondage anticipates the pattern that deliverance is often preceded by an intensifying of the very trouble it will end, a shadow of how the darkest hour before the cross, humanly speaking, preceded the greatest deliverance in history.
basic.christ: Moses' complaint, why have You brought trouble on this people, finds its answer only in what God is about to do in chapter 6, foreshadowing how the full weight of God's redemptive plan is often hidden from those living through its hardest moments, as it was even for the disciples before the resurrection.
basic.god: God allows His people to suffer worse before He delivers them, not because He is indifferent but because His timing and purposes are not always visible in the moment. He receives Moses' honest complaint without rebuking his honesty, showing that raw prayer has a place before Him.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 6:1 records God's response to this exact complaint. Romans 8:28 assures that God works all things for good even when circumstances look like they are working against His people. Psalm 13 models the same honest complaint that ends in trust.
basic.oneStory: This is the low point before the turn: Pharaoh's mockery of God's name and the increased cruelty toward Israel set the stage for the plagues that will follow, showing that the road to deliverance sometimes runs through deeper darkness first, a pattern completed at the cross before the resurrection.

context.literary:
Exodus 5 is built as a contest of voices. It opens with the messenger formula of the prophets, 'This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says,' verse 1. Within ten verses the taskmasters are using the same formula for their master: 'This is what Pharaoh says,' verse 10. Two kings issue decrees, and the chapter asks which word will stand. Pharaoh calls the LORD's word 'lies,' verse 9, literally 'words of falsehood.'

The chapter moves through three rounds of complaint, each rising higher and each ending worse. Moses and Aaron appeal to Pharaoh, verses 1 to 5, and are sent back to work. The Israelite foremen appeal to Pharaoh, verses 15 to 18, and are called slackers. The foremen then turn on Moses and Aaron, verses 20 and 21, and Moses turns to the LORD, verses 22 and 23. The complaints climb from the king's court, through the chain of command, to heaven itself.

The question 'why' runs through the chapter like a refrain. Pharaoh asks, 'why do you draw the people away?' verse 4. The taskmasters ask, 'Why have you not fulfilled your quota?' verse 14. The foremen ask Pharaoh, 'Why are you treating your servants this way?' verse 15. And Moses asks the LORD, 'why have You brought trouble upon this people?' verse 22. Everyone in the chapter is asking why, and the answer does not come until Exodus 6:1.

The chapter also reverses the ending of chapter 4. There the people believed and worshiped, 4:31. Here they blame Moses and call for God's judgment on him, 5:21. The high point of faith is followed immediately by the low point of disillusion, and the pattern of faith followed by complaint will recur through the wilderness, Exodus 14:11-12 and 16:3. The narrative is honest: a people can worship one day and despair the next.
context.historical:
Egypt's great building projects were raised largely in mudbrick. Bricks were moulded from Nile mud mixed with chopped straw, which bound the clay and helped the bricks hold together as they dried in the sun. Tomb paintings from the New Kingdom, most famously in the tomb of the vizier Rekhmire at Thebes, show foreign workers fetching water, mixing mud, moulding bricks and stacking them under overseers holding rods. The scene of Exodus 5 would have been familiar in outline to anyone who had seen a royal building site.

Exodus 1:11 says the Israelites built Pithom and Rameses as store cities, and Exodus 1:14 describes 'hard labor in brick and mortar.' Taking away the straw forced the workers to scatter across the fields to gather stubble, the rough stalks left after harvest, verse 12. That was slower and produced weaker material, while the quota stayed the same.

The administration had layers. The 'taskmasters,' verse 6, were Egyptian officials. The 'foremen,' shoterim, were Israelites appointed over their own people, verse 14, and they were beaten when the quota fell short. It was a system designed to set the oppressed against one another, and verse 21 shows it working.

Pharaoh's answer, 'Who is the LORD?' verse 2, made sense from inside Egyptian religion. Pharaoh was regarded as divine, the son of the sun god, and the upholder of cosmic order. The god of a slave people had no standing in his court. Moses would later explain that Israel's sacrifices 'would be detestable to the Egyptians,' Exodus 8:26, which may be why the request was for a journey into the wilderness. The phrase 'the people of the land,' verse 5, points to the size of the workforce: Pharaoh counts Israel as labour he cannot afford to lose even for three days.
context.canonical:
The chapter's opening question, 'Who is the LORD?' is answered by the rest of the book. God's refrain through the plagues is 'you will know that I am the LORD' or 'the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD,' Exodus 6:7, 7:5, 7:17 and 14:4. God tells Pharaoh He raised him up 'that I might display My power to you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth,' Exodus 9:16, which Paul quotes in Romans 9:17. Pharaoh's last word before the exodus is the reverse of his first: 'Go, worship the LORD as you have requested,' Exodus 12:31.

Moses' complaint in verse 22 has companions. Later, burdened with the whole people, he asks again, 'Why have You brought this trouble on Your servant?' Numbers 11:11, using the same verb. The psalmists pray in the same register: 'Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping?' Psalm 44:23, and 'How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?' Psalm 13:1. Habakkuk asks, 'How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear?' Habakkuk 1:2. Scripture gives God's people words for exactly this moment.

The image of hard labour and a heavy yoke returns in Israel's own history. Solomon's forced labour led the northern tribes to plead with Rehoboam, 'Your father put a heavy yoke on us,' 1 Kings 12:4, and his refusal split the kingdom. Israel's own kings could become Pharaohs. Psalm 81:6 remembers the exodus as God relieving Israel's shoulder of the burden and freeing their hands from the basket.

In the New Testament Jesus invites the weary and burdened to take His yoke, 'for My yoke is easy and My burden is light,' Matthew 11:28-30. The Sabbath, grounded in Deuteronomy 5:15 on Israel's slavery in Egypt, becomes in Hebrews 4:9-10 a rest that remains for the people of God. The chapter of no rest points to the rest Christ gives.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants Israel to understand that the conflict of the exodus was about lordship. Pharaoh's first words define it: 'Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice?' The ten plagues that follow are God's answer. The first hearers, having come through those plagues, were meant to see that their God had answered the question for all time, so that neither Egypt nor any later power could say again that it did not know Him.

The author also wants Israel to be honest about how deliverance began. It did not begin with relief but with worse suffering. The people turned against Moses, and Moses turned his complaint on God. The account records this without embarrassment. Israel was meant to remember that their faith had been fragile at the start, and that God's rescue did not depend on the strength of their confidence.

Finally, the author wants the chapter's unanswered question to be heard. Chapter 5 ends with Moses' accusation hanging in the air: 'You have not delivered Your people in any way.' The narrative lets that silence stand for a moment before God answers in Exodus 6:1. The hearers were meant to learn that the time between God's word and God's act can feel like His absence, and that God's answer is not to explain but to reveal Himself: 'I am the LORD,' Exodus 6:2.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes an oppressive labour policy, the collapse of a people's morale, and a prophet's accusing prayer. None of it is set out as a model for how things should be. Pharaoh's cruelty is condemned by the whole shape of the book, and the law later forbids Israel to rule harshly over one another, because they are the LORD's servants whom He brought out of Egypt, Leviticus 25:42-43.

Two things carry forward. First, obedience to God can bring immediate hardship. Moses and Aaron did exactly what God commanded, and it made things worse. Believers should not read the difficulty that follows obedience as a sign that they misheard God. God had already told Moses that Pharaoh would refuse, Exodus 3:19.

Second, the chapter permits honest lament. Moses 'returned to the LORD,' verse 22, bringing his complaint to the one who sent him rather than abandoning the mission. The psalms of lament give this kind of prayer a lasting place in worship. What the chapter does not commend is the foremen's response, which calls for God to judge His messenger, verse 21. There is a difference between wrestling with God and turning against His servants.

debates.question: Was Moses wrong to question God as he did in verse 22?

views.label: A faithful, honest lament
views.case: Moses brings his complaint directly to God rather than abandoning the mission, following a pattern of lament seen throughout the Psalms, such as Psalm 44:23-24. God responds not with rebuke but with a fuller revelation of His covenant name and plan in chapter 6.

views.label: A lapse of faith needing correction
views.case: Moses' words edge toward accusing God of failing to deliver, 'You have not delivered Your people in any way,' verse 23. Some read God's emphatic self-identification in chapter 6, 'I am the LORD,' as a needed corrective to Moses' doubt.

debates.bearing: Either reading affirms that honest struggle brought to God, rather than suppressed or taken elsewhere, is met with God's patient, self-revealing answer rather than rejection.

debates.question: Was the request for a three-day journey honest, verse 3?

views.label: A deceptive pretext
views.case: Some have argued that asking for a three-day journey, when the real goal was permanent departure to Canaan, was a ruse. On this view God permitted a stratagem against a tyrant.

views.label: A genuine, limited request that tested Pharaoh
views.case: God Himself commanded the request, Exodus 3:18, and knew Pharaoh would refuse it, 3:19. A king who would not grant even a few days of worship showed that he would never grant freedom. The modest request exposed Pharaoh's heart and left him without excuse.

views.label: An opening that God later widened
views.case: The request for worship in the wilderness was true, and the demand later becomes plain, 'Let My people go, so that they may worship Me,' Exodus 7:16. God had never promised Pharaoh that Israel would return, and the worship at Sinai was a real goal of the journey, Exodus 3:12.

debates.bearing: The text never presents the request as a lie. It was a real demand for worship, commanded by God, and its modesty made Pharaoh's refusal the more damning. The fuller demand for release follows as Pharaoh's heart is revealed.

study.originalLanguages:
Moses' first demand asks that Israel 'hold a feast' to the LORD, verse 1. The verb is chagag, from which comes chag, a pilgrimage feast. It is the word used for Israel's three annual feasts, 'Three times a year you are to celebrate a feast to Me,' Exodus 23:14. What Moses asks for is not a day off but a sacred journey to worship, a festival held in the presence of Israel's God.

Pharaoh's reply, 'I do not know the LORD,' verse 2, uses yada, to know. The verb becomes the theme of the plague narrative. God answers, 'Then you will know that I am the LORD,' Exodus 6:7, and 'the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD,' Exodus 7:5. Knowledge of God in the Old Testament is not only information; it is acknowledgment of His rule. Pharaoh's refusal to know is a refusal to submit, and the plagues will teach him by force what he would not learn by word.

Verse 9 says, 'Make the work harder on the men,' literally 'let the work be heavy,' using kaved. It is the same word that will describe Pharaoh's hardened heart, Exodus 8:15, and that Moses used of his 'slow' mouth, Exodus 4:10. Pharaoh makes Israel's labour heavy; soon his own heart will be heavy against God; and in the end the LORD will 'gain honor,' kabed, over Pharaoh, Exodus 14:4. The chapter uses the word for weight to show a contest over whose glory will prevail.

Pharaoh calls the people 'lazy,' verse 8, and 'slackers! Slackers!' verse 17. The word is raphah, to be slack or to let drop, the same verb used in Exodus 4:26 when the LORD 'let him alone.' The doubled 'slackers' in verse 17 is Pharaoh's contempt. He cannot conceive of worship as anything but idleness, because in his world the only purpose of a slave is to work.

The foremen's charge in verse 21 is vivid: 'you have made us a stench,' literally 'you have made our smell to stink,' from baash. In the first plague the same verb will describe the Nile, 'the river will stink,' Exodus 7:18. Israel feels it has become loathsome to Egypt; soon it will be Egypt's river that reeks.

Finally, verses 22 and 23 turn on two verbs. 'Why have You brought trouble,' hareota, is from raa, to do harm, and verse 23 uses the same verb of Pharaoh: 'he has brought trouble on this people.' Moses sets God and Pharaoh side by side, as though both were harming Israel. Then comes the climax: 'You have not delivered Your people in any way,' an intensive construction, hatsel lo hitsalta, literally 'delivering You have not delivered.' The verb is natsal, the very word God used at the bush, 'I have come down to rescue them,' Exodus 3:8. Moses throws God's own promise back at Him.

typology.type: Pharaoh's heavier burden before release, Exodus 5:9
typology.fulfillment: Pharaoh tightens his grip as soon as a deliverer appears. Revelation describes the same pattern at cosmic scale: 'with great fury the devil has come down to you, knowing he has only a short time,' Revelation 12:12. Herod's slaughter of the infants when the Messiah was born, Matthew 2:16, follows the same shape. The oppressor rages most when his time is short. The escalation in Christ is that the enemy's final fury at the cross became the instrument of his defeat, Colossians 2:15. Pharaoh's cruelty preceded Israel's release; Satan's served the very redemption he opposed.

typology.type: Slavery in the brick kilns, Exodus 5:6-19
typology.fulfillment: Israel labours without rest under a master who cares only for output, and no amount of effort meets the quota. Jesus describes the human condition in similar terms: 'everyone who sins is a slave to sin,' and 'if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed,' John 8:34-36. Paul writes that believers were once 'slaves to sin' and have been set free, Romans 6:17-18. The type falls short in one respect: Israel's slavery was imposed from outside, while slavery to sin is also chosen from within. Christ frees not only from the master but from the heart that served him.

typology.type: The heavy yoke and the easy yoke, Exodus 5:9 and 5:18
typology.fulfillment: Pharaoh's answer to a request for worship is more work and no rest. Jesus answers the weary with the opposite: 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest... For My yoke is easy and My burden is light,' Matthew 11:28-30. The escalation is that Jesus does not remove service altogether; He gives a different master. Israel was freed from serving Pharaoh to serve the LORD, and believers are freed from sin to become 'slaves to righteousness,' Romans 6:18. Hebrews says there remains 'a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' Hebrews 4:9.

typology.type: Moses, blamed by his people yet interceding for them, Exodus 5:21-22
typology.fulfillment: The foremen call for God to judge Moses, and Moses goes to God for them. The pattern recurs throughout his life, reaching a height after the golden calf, Exodus 32:11. Christ is the greater mediator, rejected by His own people, John 1:11, yet 'He always lives to intercede for them,' Hebrews 7:25. The contrast is sharp: Moses' prayer in Exodus 5 is partly a complaint against God, while Christ's intercession is perfectly one with the Father's will, and He is heard because of His reverence, Hebrews 5:7.

study.christ:
The chapter's opening line, 'Who is the LORD?' is the question the Gospels answer in the person of Jesus. Pharaoh refused to know the LORD; Jesus says, 'this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent,' John 17:3. Paul writes that God gave Jesus the name above every name, so that every tongue will confess that He is Lord, Philippians 2:9-11. The king who said 'I do not know the LORD' was compelled to acknowledge Him at the exodus, and every power that has asked Pharaoh's question will one day answer it on its knees.

The passage leads to Christ through the theme of rest. Pharaoh's world has no room for worship. Any pause is laziness, and the answer to a request for a feast is a heavier burden. Jesus enters a world like that and offers rest to the weary, Matthew 11:28-30. He is 'Lord of the Sabbath,' Matthew 12:8, the day that in Deuteronomy 5:15 was grounded on Israel's release from Egypt. Hebrews speaks of a Sabbath rest still remaining for God's people, Hebrews 4:9-10, a rest that Christ secures.

It leads to Christ through the darkness before deliverance. The disciples knew a moment like Exodus 5. After the cross they said, 'we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel,' Luke 24:21, words close to Moses' 'You have not delivered Your people.' Jesus had warned them: 'you will weep and wail while the world rejoices. You will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy,' John 16:20. The deepest darkness of the gospel story came just before the resurrection, as the heavier burden of Exodus 5 came just before God's mighty hand.

It leads to Christ through lament. Moses asks God why. At the cross Jesus cries, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' Matthew 27:46, quoting Psalm 22:1. The Son Himself enters the language of lament that Moses used and the psalmists prayed. The difference is decisive: Moses complains that God has not delivered, while Jesus, in His cry, bears the abandonment that makes deliverance possible. Hebrews 5:7 says He offered loud cries and tears and was heard.

Finally, the rulers who opposed God's messengers are gathered in Psalm 2, which the early church applied to Herod, Pilate and the nations who conspired against Jesus, Acts 4:25-28. They did only what God's hand had decided beforehand. Pharaoh's refusal, too, was inside God's plan, Exodus 3:19. The New Testament does not make the straw or the bricks into symbols of anything. The link with Christ is the shape of the story: God's Lordship challenged, God's people crushed and disillusioned, and God's answer arriving in power at the darkest moment.
study.god:
This chapter shows God by what He allows before it shows Him by what He does. He does not stop Pharaoh's cruelty at once. He had told Moses that Pharaoh would refuse, Exodus 3:19, and He lets the refusal play out in full. The chapter is a reminder that God's sovereignty does not mean the immediate removal of evil. He permits the oppressor to reveal himself so that His own name will be revealed more fully, Exodus 9:16.

God is also the one whose name is at stake. Pharaoh's 'Who is the LORD?' is a challenge to God's identity and authority. The whole plague narrative is God's reply, and it takes the form of self-revelation: 'I am the LORD,' Exodus 6:2, 6:6 and 6:8. When God's name is mocked, He does not argue; He acts, and by acting He makes Himself known. The doctrine of God's glory, His concern that His name be known in all the earth, is grounded here.

God is patient with His servant's complaint. Moses' prayer is sharp, even accusing. God does not strike him down or rebuke him for it. His first response is a promise, 'Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh,' Exodus 6:1, and then a renewed revelation of His name and His covenant, 6:2-8. The God who was angry at Moses' refusal to go, Exodus 4:14, is patient with Moses' pain in going. He distinguishes between unbelief that refuses the mission and anguish that brings its questions to Him.

God is also the God who uses darkness. The worsening of Israel's condition sets up the stage for His power. Every plague will be the more obviously His because there was no human hope left. In Scripture God often lets His people reach the end of their own resources before He acts, as at the sea, where Israel was trapped between the army and the water, Exodus 14:10-14.

The chapter holds a tension that Scripture does not resolve cheaply. God has seen, heard and come down, Exodus 3:7-8, yet His people suffer more. Moses feels the contradiction and says so. The answer is not that God's compassion was false, but that His timing and His purpose were larger than Moses could see. 'Our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal glory,' Paul would later write, 2 Corinthians 4:17.

For worship, the chapter teaches believers that lament is a form of faith. Moses 'returned to the LORD,' verse 22. The God who hears the cries of the oppressed also hears the complaints of His servants, and He answers with Himself.

crossReferences.note: God's answer to Moses' complaint. He does not explain the delay but promises, 'Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh,' and then reveals His name and covenant again: I am the LORD, I will bring you out, I will redeem you, I will take you as My people. Chapter 5's question is answered by God's self-revelation.

The Egyptians made Israel's lives bitter with hard labour in brick and mortar. Chapter 5 intensifies the oppression first described there. The straw policy is not a new cruelty so much as the same cruelty made heavier in response to God's claim on His people.

God tells Pharaoh, 'I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power to you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.' Pharaoh's 'Who is the LORD?' in 5:2 becomes the occasion for the LORD to make Himself known across the world.

Pharaoh's final words: 'Go, worship the LORD as you have requested... And bless me also.' The king who said 'I do not know the LORD' and 'I will not let Israel go' now sends them out and asks for a blessing. The contest begun in chapter 5 ends in Pharaoh's surrender.

Moses, overwhelmed by the people's complaints, asks, 'Why have You brought this trouble on Your servant?' using the same verb as Exodus 5:22. Moses' prayer life keeps returning to honest lament, and God again answers with provision, sharing the burden with seventy elders.

'Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping?... Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction and oppression?' The psalmist prays Moses' prayer for a later generation. Scripture preserves this kind of lament as part of Israel's worship, not as a failure of faith.

The prophet asks how long he must cry for help without being heard. Like Moses, Habakkuk sees injustice increasing and brings his protest to God. Both prophets receive an answer that does not remove the tension at once but reveals God's larger purpose and calls for faith.

The northern tribes plead with Rehoboam that his father Solomon put a heavy yoke on them. Israel's own king had begun to act like Pharaoh. The memory of Exodus 5 made forced labour under an Israelite king a bitter irony, and Rehoboam's harshness divided the kingdom.

Jesus invites the weary and burdened to take His yoke, which is easy, and His burden, which is light. Pharaoh answered a request for worship with a heavier load. Jesus answers weariness with rest, and His service is the rest that Pharaoh's world could never give.

The disciples on the road to Emmaus say, 'we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel.' Like Moses in Exodus 5:23, they feel that God's promised deliverance has failed. In both cases the darkest moment comes just before God's decisive act of redemption.

Jesus tells His disciples they will grieve while the world rejoices, but their grief will turn to joy. The pattern of Exodus 5, where things get worse before God acts, is the pattern of the cross and resurrection. Sorrow is real, but it gives way to a joy no one can take away.

'There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God.' Israel in Exodus 5 was denied even three days to worship. The rest God gave at Sinai, grounded in Israel's release from Egypt, Deuteronomy 5:15, points to a final rest into which believers enter through Christ.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God made humanity to work the ground and keep it, and He rested on the seventh day, Genesis 2:2-3 and 2:15. Work and rest belonged together, and both were ordered toward God. After the fall, work became painful toil, Genesis 3:17-19. Exodus 5 shows toil at its worst: work without rest, under a master who calls worship idleness and answers a plea for a feast with a heavier load.

The chapter also recalls Babel. The builders there said, 'Come, let us make bricks,' and set out to make a name for themselves, Genesis 11:3-4. Now Israel makes bricks for a king who thinks he answers to no god. Human empires keep building with brick and ambition, and they keep enslaving others to do it. Pharaoh's question, 'Who is the LORD?' is the question of every empire that has tried to make a name for itself without God.

Exodus 5 sets up everything that follows. Because Pharaoh refuses to know the LORD, the LORD will make Himself known in the plagues, the Passover and the sea. Israel will be brought out to worship at Sinai and given a Sabbath rooted in their release, Deuteronomy 5:15. Their law will forbid them to become Pharaohs to one another. Yet their own kings will lay heavy yokes on them, 1 Kings 12:4, and they will go into exile, needing a greater exodus.

The story finds its centre in Jesus, who calls the weary to rest, Matthew 11:28, and who passed through the darkest hour, crying 'why?' on the cross, Matthew 27:46, before God's mighty hand raised Him. The disciples, like Moses, thought deliverance had failed, Luke 24:21. It had not. It had arrived.

The story ends in the new creation, where God's people 'will not labor in vain,' Isaiah 65:23, and where Pharaoh's question is answered by every creature. 'There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' Hebrews 4:9. The redeemed will serve God, and His servants 'will worship Him' and 'see His face,' Revelation 22:3-4. The feast Moses asked Pharaoh to allow in the wilderness becomes the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9, and no taskmaster will ever interrupt it.

quiz.q: How did Pharaoh respond to Moses and Aaron's first request?

options.text: He agreed immediately to let Israel go.
options.note: Pharaoh flatly refused; his agreement comes only after many plagues, much later in the narrative.

options.text: He asked for more information before deciding.
options.note: His response was outright refusal, not a request for more information.

options.text: He mocked the LORD's name and refused, saying he did not know the LORD.
options.note: Verse 2 records Pharaoh's exact, contemptuous words.

options.text: He punished Moses and Aaron personally on the spot.
options.note: His punishment fell on the Israelite laborers, not directly on Moses and Aaron in this scene.

quiz.q: What new policy did Pharaoh impose after Moses and Aaron's request?

options.text: The Israelites had to gather their own straw for bricks while keeping the same daily quota.
options.note: Verses 6 to 9 describe this harsher policy exactly.

options.text: He released a portion of the Israelites immediately.
options.note: No release occurred; the labor became harsher, not lighter.

options.text: He reduced their workload as a goodwill gesture.
options.note: The opposite happened; the workload effectively increased.

options.text: He made no changes to their labor at all.
options.note: A specific, harsher new policy was imposed.

quiz.q: Who did the Israelite foremen blame for their increased suffering?

options.text: No one; they accepted the situation without complaint.
options.note: Their complaint to Moses and Aaron is explicit and sharp.

options.text: Moses and Aaron, saying they had made them a stench before Pharaoh.
options.note: Verse 21 records the foremen's direct accusation against Moses and Aaron.

options.text: Themselves, for not working hard enough.
options.note: They placed the blame on Moses and Aaron's actions, not on their own effort.

options.text: Pharaoh alone, with no blame directed at Moses.
options.note: The foremen specifically confronted and blamed Moses and Aaron, not only Pharaoh.

quiz.q: How did Moses respond to the foremen's accusation?

options.text: He had no reaction recorded.
options.note: His anguished prayer to God is explicitly recorded.

options.text: He gave up the mission entirely.
options.note: Moses continues in his role; the following chapter shows God renewing the mission, not Moses abandoning it.

options.text: He returned to the LORD and asked why He had brought trouble on the people and had not yet delivered them.
options.note: Verses 22 to 23 record Moses' honest, anguished complaint directly to God.

options.text: He rebuked the foremen harshly and walked away.
options.note: The text records Moses taking the complaint to God, not rebuking the foremen.

quiz.q: What does this chapter teach about the path to deliverance?

options.text: God abandoned His people at this point in the story.
options.note: The following chapter shows God renewing His promise, not abandoning His people.

options.text: This chapter has no bearing on the theme of deliverance.
options.note: The chapter is central to the tension and timing of the whole deliverance narrative.

options.text: Obedience always brings instant relief from hardship.
options.note: This chapter shows the opposite: obedience is followed by harsher bondage before deliverance.

options.text: Obedience to God's call can bring intensified suffering before deliverance comes, not immediate relief.
options.note: The chapter shows things getting harder, not easier, right after Moses obeys God's command to confront Pharaoh.

questions: Pharaoh mocked the LORD's name and refused to listen. Where do you encounter dismissiveness toward God's authority in your own life or culture, and how does that shape how you respond?
Obeying God's call led to harsher circumstances for Israel, not immediate relief. Have you experienced a season where following God seemed to make things worse before they got better?
The foremen blamed Moses for their suffering, when the fault truly lay with Pharaoh's cruelty. Where might you be misdirecting blame toward the wrong source when circumstances feel unbearable?
Moses brought his raw, honest complaint directly to God rather than hiding it or giving up. What honest question or complaint do you need to bring to God in prayer this week?
This dark chapter is answered by God's renewed promise in chapter 6. What current struggle do you need to trust God is about to answer, even though you cannot yet see how?

translationNotes.note: Pharaoh's question, who is the LORD, uses the covenant name YHWH, showing his contempt is aimed specifically at Israel's God by name, not merely at a generic deity.

The phrase pay no attention to these lies reflects Pharaoh's characterization of Israel's request to worship as a deceptive pretext, though the text has already shown the request came directly from the LORD's own instruction.
